title: Stored agricultural product pest fumigation management

lessons.title: Stored product pests and when to fumigate
lessons.html:
Protecting the national grain store

South Africa stores millions of tons of maize, wheat, sorghum, soybeans and sunflower each year in concrete silos, steel bins, bunkers and bag stores, as well as dried fruit, nuts, tobacco and animal feeds. Insects can reduce grain mass and quality, raise temperature and moisture, encourage moulds and cause rejection by millers, feed manufacturers and export buyers. Fumigation is the main method of disinfesting stored commodities, but it is only one part of a stored product management programme.

Key stored product insects

  • Primary pests that attack whole kernels: maize weevil and rice weevil, lesser grain borer, Angoumois grain moth.
  • Secondary pests that feed on damaged grain, dust and processed products: red flour beetle, confused flour beetle, sawtoothed grain beetle, Indian meal moth.
  • Mites in damp commodities.

Primary pests develop hidden inside kernels, so contact insecticides cannot reach all stages. A fumigant gas can penetrate the kernels.

Prevention first

  • Clean empty bins, conveyors, pits and surrounding areas before intake.
  • Dry grain to safe storage moisture and cool it with aeration.
  • Use registered grain protectants on intake where appropriate and permitted by the buyer.
  • Do not mix old, infested grain with new grain.
  • Monitor regularly with probes, traps, sieving and temperature cables.

Deciding to fumigate

Fumigation is justified when monitoring shows live insects at or above the agreed threshold, before outloading to a buyer who requires insect-free grain, or to meet phytosanitary requirements for export. Consider the commodity, storage period remaining, temperature, whether the structure can be made gas-tight and the buyer's residue requirements.

Fumigants for stored products

Phosphine, generated from aluminium or magnesium phosphide formulations or supplied as cylinder gas, is the main fumigant for stored grain. It leaves low residues when correctly used, but it is slow-acting and needs adequate exposure time and temperature as the label specifies. Only operators registered for fumigation under Act 36 of 1947 may fumigate for reward.

lessons.title: Sealing, dosing and the problem of resistance
lessons.html:
Gas-tightness decides success

Phosphine resistance in stored product insects is a recognised problem in many countries. The main cause is repeated fumigation in leaky structures: insects survive low concentrations, and survivors breed. A fumigation that does not hold the label concentration for the full exposure period is not only wasteful; it actively makes future control harder.

Structures and sealing

Storage typeSealing approach
Concrete silo binsSeal top hatches, spout openings and bottom slides; check cracks and joints
Steel binsSeal eaves gaps, aeration fans and ducts, roof vents and doors; many older bins are not designed to be gas-tight
Bag stacksCover with gas-proof sheets sealed to the floor with sand snakes
BunkersGas-tight covers sealed at the edges
Containers and ship holdsSeal doors and vents; follow specialist procedures

Where possible, pressure-test sealed structures before fumigation. A structure that cannot be sealed adequately should not be fumigated; alternative measures or transfer to a sealable structure should be considered.

Calculating and applying the dose

  1. Calculate the volume of the structure or enclosure, or the tonnage, as the label requires.
  2. Determine the dose and minimum exposure period from the label, considering the grain temperature.
  3. Distribute the product as the label specifies: probing tablets into the grain mass, placing sachets or blankets on the surface or in the airstream, or recirculating gas.
  4. Keep phosphide products away from water and liquids; contact with water can cause rapid gas release and fire.
  5. Seal the final openings immediately after application.

Recirculation

In tall silos gas may not distribute evenly. Recirculation systems move gas through the bulk to achieve a uniform concentration. Monitor at several depths to confirm distribution.

Monitoring concentration

Use sampling lines placed before application and suitable instruments to measure concentration at intervals. Record readings and compare them with the label requirements. If the concentration falls, find and fix the leak; do not simply shorten or end the fumigation.

lessons.title: Safety, aeration and record keeping
lessons.html:
Protecting people on a silo complex

Silo complexes are busy workplaces with weighbridges, offices, truck queues and workers moving between bins. Phosphine travels through conveyors, tunnels, elevator legs and connected bins into areas where people work.

Safety measures

  • Establish an exclusion zone around the fumigated structure and any connected spaces; isolate interconnecting conveyors and ducts.
  • Post warning signs at all access points with fumigant, date, time and emergency contact.
  • Inform the site manager, shift supervisors and workers; restrict entry to authorised fumigation personnel.
  • Monitor gas in adjacent work areas, tunnels and offices during the exposure.
  • Work in teams of at least two with respiratory protection as the label requires, and with a standby person.
  • Have emergency procedures, the label and SDS, and contact details for emergency medical services readily available.

Aeration and outloading

At the end of the exposure period, aerate as planned, using aeration fans where available, while maintaining the exclusion zone. Test concentrations in the headspace and in the grain before allowing entry or outloading. Grain may release gas when moved, so test during initial outloading and protect workers at transfer points.

Residues and disposal

Spent phosphide residues may still contain unreacted material. Collect them and deactivate or dispose of them strictly according to the label. Never put residues in closed containers, bins or drains without following the label.

Evaluating the fumigation

After aeration, sample the grain and check for live insects at all stages, using incubation of samples if required. A successful fumigation kills all life stages. Survivors indicate that concentration or exposure was inadequate, or that resistance may be present; report this and review the method.

Records

Keep a fumigation record: commodity, quantity, structure, date and time of application, product and registration number, dose, temperature, concentration readings, exposure period, aeration and clearance times, and operator names and registration. These records are needed for buyers, export certification and audits.

Key points

  • Prevention, monitoring and thresholds come before fumigation.
  • Primary pests develop inside kernels, which is why a penetrating gas is used.
  • Leaky structures cause failure and drive phosphine resistance; do not fumigate structures that cannot be sealed.
  • Keep phosphide products away from water and monitor concentrations throughout exposure.
  • Protect connected work areas, test before outloading and keep full fumigation records.
